![The finished project](finished-wall.jpeg)

When we bought our house in Watertown, Massachusetts at the end
of 2023, it was just about perfect, at least from our point of
view. The house was built in the 1920s and had historic character, but
it had also been renovated and updated with modern appliances,
heating, cooling, and water systems. It has beautiful trees and a nice
backyard, but it is also in a relatively dense urban setting right
next to Cambridge and just across the Charles River from Boston.

As part of the renovation before we bought the house the top floor
attic had been converted into a master suite with its own bathroom and
small outdoor deck with a view of the neighborhood and Watertown's
athletic fields. The only downside of the master suite was that there
was only a half wall and no door between the bedroom and stairway to
the second floor. We occasionally found that it would be nice to have
a bit more privacy and soundproofing, especially when we had family
and visitors staying with us.

![Our master bedroom showing the half wall and landing open to the stairway and second floor](39-8-Lovell-master-balcony-door.jpeg)

After a couple of years we decided that it was time to take action and
to build out a full wall with a door. One concern was to avoid making
the room seem darker and smaller. We decided to put a window in the
wall (we ended up with stained glass) and to install a mostly glass
door, similar to the existing balcony door. The glass door and stained
glass window would allow light to pass in both directions between the
bedroom with its two skylights and two windows, and the stair landing
with its glass door looking out at the balcony and surrounding trees.

I started by getting out some graph paper and taking a first set of
measurements.

![The initial set of measurements](initial-measurements.jpeg)

One of the interesting things I found from the first set of
measurements is that the corner of the wall across from the stairs did
not quite line up with the half wall. The difference ended up being
half an inch (76.75" - (36.75" + 39.5")). This resulted in a little
corner in the wall once everything was completed. 

## So many angles

The most complicated part of the design and building process was the
two different slanting roof angles joined by a central flat
beam.

![A worksheet for working out roof, wall, and framing angles](measurements-with-angles.jpeg)

Eventually I ended up modeling it out in the SketchUp 3-D CAD program,
which allowed me to visualize both the before and after states in relatively high fidelity.

![The before version of the Sketchup model](sketchup-3d-before.jpeg)

![An initial as-designed view in Sketchup](sketchup-3d-design.png)

## Tying into the existing structure

I needed to figure out where studs, beams, and joists were in the
existing structure to allow sturdy attachment of the new structure to
the existing structure. Stud finder devices and drilling little holes
were somewhat helpful, but I ended up removing some squares of
wallboard to get a full view of what was available. All of the test
holes were covered up by new framing and drywall.

![Viewing holes cut into the drywall to see the existing structure](view-holes-to-establish-structure.jpeg)

I originally thought that I was going to need something wider than a
two-by-four to overlap enough with the existing structure, but I was able
to do everything with two-by-fours, which resulted in a much better-looking
final product.

## Framing

I used a combination of digital and analog models to estimate the
number of two-by-fours I would need to buy. I printed out a view of the
Sketchup model and then drew on it with a pencil.

![A combined Sketchup and pencil drawing to estimate the number of two-by-fours](lumber-estimation-worksheet.jpeg)

The first round of framing went quickly. I centered the framing on the
existing half wall to achieve a flat wall on both sides. I used an old
and very basic laser level to shoot lines across the door opening. I
thought about springing for one of the fancier laser levels, but the
old one ended up working well enough.

![The initial framing up to the point of door and window framing](inital-framing.jpeg)

I framed the door and window openings a few days later. As usual, the
trickiest part was the ceiling angle and how it forced the header at
the top of the door opening to be cut at the same slightly-sloping
angle.

Next came the drywall, which was the first part of the project that
required me to work from the back side of the wall where there is a
significant drop down to the second floor, requiring a ladder to do
the work.

![The back side of the framing from the landing and stairs side](door-and-window-framing-from-landing.jpeg)

## Drywall installation 

The two hardest parts about putting up the drywall were:

1. Funky angles, notches, and cut-outs needed on the roof line, and
2. Standing on a ladder to place and fasten the drywall from the
   stairway side of the wall.
   
![Bedroom-side drywall](drywall-1.jpeg)

![Stairway-adjacent drywall](drywall-2.jpeg)

![Landing drywall](drywall-3.jpeg)

## Door and window installation 

I decided to spring for a pre-hung door because I was already pushing
the limits of my interior framing experience. I watched several door
installation videos on YouTube and got myself a longer level, which allowed me
to get the door level and plumb, and open and close easily.

![Using shims to level and plumb the door](door-hanging.jpeg)

We used an opaque stained glass window to allow light through while
still providing privacy. The glass was sold as a decorative hanging,
but worked well in this slightly different application.

![We used a piece of glass originally intended as a decorative hanging](stained-glass-window.jpeg)

## Taping, mudding, and trim

I had no experience taping and mudding drywall, so I watched a lot of
videos and put off that part of the project for a few weeks. We were
already able to use the door and enjoy the extra privacy.

The taping and mudding was the messiest part of the process, primarily
because of the required sanding to end up with smooth, flat surfaces.

Installing the trim was much easier, from my point of view. The
trickier areas were around the stained glass window, which required
more care and pieces of wood than I had originally planned, and the
little corner caused by the half-inch misalignment between the
original half wall and the landing corner, which required some custom
angling and shimming of the trim to make a nice joint. 

## Painting 

I needed three colors and types of paint:

1. Wall
2. Trim
3. Ceiling

Even though there wasn't a lot of area to cover, the multiple angles
and surfaces led to several partial days of painting. 

## The finished product 

We are really happy with the appearance and functionality of the new wall,
window, and door. It functions exactly as intended and it matches the
existing look of the rest of the house. I also ended up putting some
existing skills to use and learning a bunch of new ones.

![The finished wall, door, and window](finished-product-bedroom-side.jpeg)

![The finished wall from the landing and stairwell](finished-product-stairway.jpeg)

We ended up putting in some new cabinet storage against the new wall.

![Our new cabinet storage against the wall](new-bedroom-storage.jpeg)
